text.p: Seventeen-year-old Olga Khristoforova swooped to snatch the women's highboard diving gold which fellow Russian Evgenia Olshevskaya let slip from her grasp at the European swimming championships on Thursday.

Khristoforova, who had trailed for most of the two days of competition, pulled off a superb final dive which thrust her from fifth to first in a final of fluctuating fortunes beneath a scorching sun at the San Pablo pool.

Earlier, Germany's Andreas Wels claimed the first gold of the 12-day championships, winning from compatriot Holger Schlepps and Spain's home hope Rafael Alvarez in the men's one-metre springboard final.
Wels, fourth at the last European championships in Vienna in 1995, always looked a strong contender for gold but Khristoforova's victory capped an afternoon of surprises on the women's highboard.
Khristoforova, ninth of the 12 qualifiers, held her nerve on the hugely demanding backward 1-1/2 somersaults with 3-1/2 twists which earned her gold and 71.04 points, the highest mark of the final.
Olshevskaya, 18, had looked the more likely member of Russia's new diving generation to win the title on the 10-metre platform but threw it away in the final round.
She had led after the second and fourth rounds of the five-round final and had brought the highest total into the final from the four dives of the morning session which counted in the classification.
But Olshevskaya faltered when it mattered most and her execution of the dive which brought glory to her team mate proved her own undoing.
She netted a meagre 33.60 points and slipped out of the medals from first to fifth.
Khristoforova amassed 441.60 points from the day's nine dives to win the closely fought contest.
Olympic silver medallist Annika Walter of Germany gained one more silver (438.66), just pipping Ukraine's Svetlana Serbina (438.51).
Wels, first in the preliminary round and his semifinal, compiled 362.10 points from his six dives in the six-man one-metre springboard final.
Schlepps took the silver with 357.12. Alvarez, who had beaten Schlepps in winning his morning semifinal, had to settle for bronze with 355.56.

Confusion was caused by the failure of the electronic scoring system on the opening dive of the men's final and intermittently during the first three rounds of dives. Old-fashioned scorecards came to the rescue.
